title: Select is switch/case for concurrency!
text:
Animals explain the select concurrency statement


An early try at programming-with-cartoons, in the spirit of _why’s Poignant Guide. Current work is at home.


read the transcript!


bubble 1: guy asks bird

What is select?

bubble 2: bird explains

It’s a control structure for concurrency. And Rob Pike, one of Golang’s developers, says it’s the reason channels and goroutines are built-in to the language.

bubble 3: guy asks “how does it work?”

Bird answers “It waits until 1 channel is ready. Kind of like case, and then runs the code in the corresponding branch.”

bubble 4: bird explains lines in Rob Pike’s example

{% highlight golang linenos %} select { case v1 := <-c1: fmt.Printf(“received %v from c1”, v1) case v2 := <-c2: // bird says here it is fanning in from c1 and c2 to stdout fmt.Printf(“received %v from c2”, v1) case c3 <- 23: fmt.Printf(“sent %v to c3”, 23) default: // giraffe says you can give a default if no channel is ready fmt.Printf(“no one was ready to communicate”) } {% endhighlight %}
Finally a cow explains if more than 1 channel is ready, then select picks on branch pseudorandomly.

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
So many money questions: my drawing, made to talk with Runway Act-Two.
Who this is for: Percentages (spreadsheet) · Logarithms (a little Python) · Differential equations

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
Guess first
Let’s say we had $500,000 and we want to spend $20,000 a year. Well, then we know that in 25 years we’ll run out of money. It’ll all be gone.
We’ve also heard of interest. If we put the $500,000 in a bank, we’ll get some more money every year. So what if we were to make 2% interest every year? Will the money last longer than 25 years, if we spend $20,000 a year?
Now, another thing that happens over the years, especially over, say, 25 years, is that things get more expensive. 25 years ago, a meal probably cost a lot less. You could probably get french fries and a hamburger for $5, and today that might cost $10. If you are buying hamburgers, you may have to spend more each year. That’s called inflation.
But you might be getting money from interest, and the money you get from interest might be a little more than the money you have to spend from inflation. Suppose your money earns 5% interest and there’s 4% inflation. Then in a real sense you’re getting 1% more value per year. So how does that affect how long the money will last?
Remember, in this second part you’re not spending $20,000 a year. You’re spending $20,000 worth every year, based on the first year’s prices.
Write your guesses down before reading on. Nobody will check them. That’s the point.

Where to now? Both roads end up in the same place.

Did people 800 years ago worry about this too?
I just want to see if my guess was right.

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
section: Meet the man who asked first
text:
Meet the man who asked first



Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci. The picture is from 1850, so it’s a bit of a guess what he might have looked like. (Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.)


Most people know Fibonacci for coming up with a sequence where you take the two previous numbers and add them. You might start with 1, 1. Add them, you get 2. Then you add the two previous ones: 1 plus 2 is 3, 2 plus 3 is 5. So the Fibonacci sequence is 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …
It has a lot of interesting history and all kinds of deep connections. It connects out to something called the golden ratio, which is what makes certain things look very aesthetic. They say the Parthenon follows the golden ratio in terms of its height versus its width. I’m not sure why, but that’s what I’ve found out.
But what’s interesting here is his Liber Abaci (“The Book of Calculation”). He wrote it in 1202, so this is a long time ago. It was where he showed merchants, Italian merchants, how to use Hindu–Arabic numerals to find profits, convert money from one country’s currency to another’s, and work out interest. And interest is what we’re looking at here.
Somewhere in there is a problem that’s basically ours: someone has money in the bank and takes a fixed amount out each year. When does it run out?

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
Build it in a spreadsheet
Download the spreadsheet.
Click on the spreadsheet and see how your guess works out.
What’s great about a spreadsheet is that it’s a table, but you can change the numbers at the top. What if you start with $100,000 instead of $500,000? What if you start with $100? What if you were getting more interest? What if you’re getting less interest? You can change all the numbers at the top, and the great thing about spreadsheets is that everything changes. It lets you see when it turns red, when the money would run out. And if you actually spend less or get more interest, you might never run out of money, which is a good thing.

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
The pattern
At $5,000 a year the balance never moves, because you’re spending exactly the interest (1% of $500,000 = $5,000). Spend less than the interest and the pile grows forever. Spend more and it shrinks, and it shrinks faster each year, because a smaller pile earns less interest. That’s why the last few years of the spreadsheet drop so steeply.






NotePercentages · Try it



Your spreadsheet has a “Continuous formula” cell up top that says the money lasts about 28.8 years. Your table ran out in year 29. Two completely different methods agree. Whenever two methods agree, you can trust both a bit more. You’ll use this trick all through the book.



The crossroads. You have the whole idea now, and stopping here is a complete chapter. If one of these questions is nagging at you, follow it. Every box ends with a way back here.

Could I get the answer on a calculator in one step? logarithms · a little Python
How can adding numbers up forever give an ordinary number? geometric series
What if the stock market crashes the year I start spending? simulation · Python
What if the money grew every second, not once a year? differential equations
Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot? no new math



Or a question about the machine:

How does a chatbot choose its next word? exponentials · a little Python
Can anyone see what’s going on inside when it adds? interpretability








NoteLogarithms · a formula instead of a table





The table works, but it takes 29 rows. The shortcut needs two functions from precalculus.
The exponential is one of the most important functions in business because it represents continuously compounded return
\[
FV = PV e^{rt}
\]
We begin with logarithms, which are the inverse of the exponential. In this course, just like we use \(e\) as the default base for an exponential function, we use the natural log \(\ln\) as the default logarithm.
With those two, the table collapses into one line:
\[
T = \frac{1}{r}\,\ln\!\frac{c}{c - rW}
\]
where \(W\) is the nest egg, \(c\) is yearly spending and \(r\) is the interest rate (as a decimal). With our numbers, \(T = 100 \ln(20000/15000) \approx 28.8\) years.
Notice what happens when \(c = rW\) (spending equals interest): the bottom of the fraction is zero, and the formula says “forever”. That’s the pattern you found in the spreadsheet.
Here’s the same thing in Python, checked against the year-by-year method:

from math import log

W0, c, r = 500_000, 20_000, 0.01

# year by year, like the spreadsheet
W, years = W0, 0
while W > 0:
    W = W * (1 + r) - c
    years += 1

T = log(c / (c - r * W0)) / r      # the shortcut formula
print(f"year by year: runs out during year {years}")
print(f"formula:      T = {T:.1f} years")

year by year: runs out during year 29
formula:      T = 28.8 years



Next: How can adding up forever give an ordinary number? · What if the money grew every second? · ↩︎ Back to the crossroads










NoteSoftmax · how a chatbot turns scores into odds





A chatbot writes one token at a time. At each step it gives every token in its dictionary a score: bigger means “more likely to come next”. Scores can be any number, even negative, so they aren’t probabilities yet.
To turn scores into probabilities it uses the same \(e\) as continuous compounding. Raise \(e\) to each score, then divide by the total:
\[
p_i = \frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}}
\]
This is called softmax. The exponential makes every number positive, and dividing by the total makes them add up to 1. And just as compounding turns a small difference in interest rate into a big difference in money, the exponential turns a small lead in score into a big lead in probability: a score 1 higher means \(e \approx 2.7\) times as likely.
Here the model has just written “The money will last 28.” and is choosing the next token:

from math import exp

scores = {"8": 3.0, "9": 2.0, "7": 1.0, "5": -1.0}   # made-up scores

total = sum(exp(s) for s in scores.values())
probs = {tok: exp(s) / total for tok, s in scores.items()}
for tok, p in probs.items():
    print(f"'{tok}': {p:.3f}")

# second check: probabilities add to 1, and a score 1 higher is e times as likely
print(f"sum = {sum(probs.values()):.6f}")
print(f"p('8') / p('9') = {probs['8'] / probs['9']:.4f}  vs  e = {exp(1):.4f}")

'8': 0.657
'9': 0.242
'7': 0.089
'5': 0.012
sum = 1.000000
p('8') / p('9') = 2.7183  vs  e = 2.7183


So the model will most likely write “28.8”, but about one time in four it writes “28.9”, which is where the confident-but-wrong answers come from. Some chatbots let you set a temperature: dividing every score by a number bigger than 1 flattens the differences, so the model takes more chances.

↩︎ Back to the crossroads · Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot?










NoteSeries · why the table has a formula at all





Each year the money you still have grows by a factor of \(1.01\), and another $20,000 comes out. Add up all those withdrawals and their lost interest and you get a geometric series.
A series is the sum of a sequence — an infinite sum. The sum of an infinite list of numbers can either be finite, so the series can converge to a number, or the sum can be infinite, so the series diverges.
We start with the basic geometric series:
\[S = 1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4+\cdots\]
Here \(r\) is a constant, the series converges when \(|r|<1\) and diverges when \(1\leq|r|\). In fact, we can find what number the infinite geometric series converges to. Write the series out for \(Sr\):
\[Sr = r+r^2+r^3+r^4+r^5+\cdots\]
Looks a lot like the series for \(S\) itself. Now subtract:
\[S-Sr=1\]
All the terms cancel! And then solve for \(S\):
\[S=\frac1{1-r}=1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4+\cdots\]
Now that we know \(S\), we can easily find other finite sums like
\[1+r+r^2+\cdots+r^{321}=S-Sr^{322}=S(1-r^{322})=\frac{1-r^{322}}{1-r}\]
For the money, the ratio is \(1.01\) instead of \(r\), and we stop after \(n\) years instead of going on forever. Set the balance to zero and solve for \(n\):
\[
n = \frac{\ln\big(c/(c - rW)\big)}{\ln(1+r)} = \frac{\ln(4/3)}{\ln 1.01} \approx 28.9 \text{ years,}
\]
which matches the spreadsheet (year 29) even better than the continuous 28.8.

Next: What if the money grew every second? · ↩︎ Back to the crossroads










NoteSimulation · what if returns are random?





Real investments don’t pay a steady 1%. Some years are great, some are terrible. Let’s say returns average 3% but swing a lot, then simulate 10,000 possible futures and count how many run out within 30 years:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, years = 10_000, 30
returns = rng.normal(0.03, 0.12, size=(n, years))

W = np.full(n, 500_000.0)
paths = np.empty((n, years))
for t in range(years):
    W = np.maximum(W * (1 + returns[:, t]) - 20_000, 0)
    paths[:, t] = W

print(f"ran out within {years} years: {(paths[:, -1] == 0).mean():.1%}")

plt.plot(paths[:50].T / 1000, lw=0.7, alpha=0.6)
plt.xlabel("year"); plt.ylabel("balance ($ thousands)")
plt.title("50 of the 10,000 simulated futures");

ran out within 30 years: 36.5%









The average return (3%) is higher than before, yet about a third of the futures still run dry. Bad years early on hurt the most, because they shrink the pile right when it has the most growing left to do.

Next: What if the money grew every second? · ↩︎ Back to the crossroads · Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot?










NoteDifferential equations · where the formula comes from





Treat time as continuous. The balance changes at the rate interest in minus spending out:
\[
\frac{dW}{dt} = rW - c, \qquad W(0) = W_0 .
\]
That’s a differential equation.
If \(f(x)\) is a function, then \(f'(x)\) or \(df/dx\) is its derivative. We can make equations involving them. In these equations, we solve for \(f(x)\) using integration. We can also plug in functions by taking their derivatives to see whether they satisfy a differential equation.
For instance, we can look at the equation \(f' = k f\), and then we can try \(f=\cos(x)\). Then \(f'(x)=-\sin(x)\), so when we plug in we get \(\cos(x)=-k\sin(x)\). These are unequal so \(f=\cos(x)\) does not solve the equation. Next we can try \(f=e^{kx}\) so that \(f'=k e^{kx}\). Plugging in we get \(ke^{kx}=k e^{kx}\) so that \(f=e^{kx}\) does solve the equation.
Our money equation is almost \(f' = kf\), just with the \(-c\) tacked on. So try an exponential plus a constant, and plug in. It works:
\[
W(t) = \frac{c}{r} + \left(W_0 - \frac{c}{r}\right)e^{rt}.
\]
Set \(W(T) = 0\) and solve for \(T\) to get the logarithm formula. The quantity \(c/r\) is the balance whose interest exactly pays for the spending: start above it and you grow forever, start below it and you hit zero.
Your spreadsheet was solving this equation all along.



Leonhard Euler in 1753, pastel by Jakob Emanuel Handmann. He had already lost the sight of his right eye in the late 1730s, and went on to publish more mathematics than almost anyone in history. (Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.)


A differential equation \(y'(x)=f(x,y)\) specifies the slope of a solution curve \(y(x)\) at any point \((x,y)\) in the plane. Suppose we want to estimate the solution \(y(x)\) with a given initial value \(y(x_0)=y_0\). This can be done more simply by realizing that the slope is the “rise-over-run”, so the \(\Delta y = f(x,y)\Delta x\) is how much the \(y\) increases when we take a step \(\Delta x\).
For us \(f = rW - c\) and the step is one year, so \(\Delta W = rW - c\): interest minus spending, which is exactly one row of the spreadsheet. The 29-row table is Euler’s method with \(\Delta t = 1\). That’s why it lands close to, but not exactly on, the continuous answer of 28.8 years.
The random version, where returns are noisy and your lifetime is uncertain too, is Milevsky’s seventh equation, named for Andrey Kolmogorov. It gives the probability of outliving your money.

↩︎ Back to the crossroads · Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot?










NoteInterpretability · watching a model add





Can we look inside a model and see how it does a sum? A new field called interpretability tries to do exactly that. Researchers trace which parts of the model light up, and what each part contributes, as it works.
In 2025, researchers at Anthropic traced one of their models adding \(36 + 59\). It didn’t carry the one. It ran two paths side by side:

one path made a rough estimate of the size, something like “a bit over 90”;
another worked out only the last digit exactly: 6 + 9 ends in 5.

Put together, “a bit over 90” and “ends in 5” give 95. That’s a strange way to add, but it works, and nobody taught it that. It found the method on its own while learning to predict text.
Here’s the part worth remembering. When they then asked the model how it got 95, it described the school method: add the ones, carry the one, add the tens. Its explanation was a sensible story, but it wasn’t what it had actually done.
So checking a chatbot means checking two things: its answer (against your spreadsheet) and its explanation (which may be a plausible story rather than a report).

↩︎ Back to the crossroads · Couldn’t I just ask a chatbot?

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
Using AI
Ask an AI assistant: “I have $500,000, spend $20,000 a year and earn 1%. How many years will it last?”
Then check its answer against your spreadsheet. AI chatbots are often shaky at arithmetic, even when they sound very sure of themselves. If it’s wrong, can you work out what it did? Now ask it to write a spreadsheet formula or Python code for the problem instead of answering directly, and check that. Which way worked better?

What the chatbot sees
When you type “I have $500,000”, the chatbot never sees the number the way you do. Before anything else happens, your text is chopped into tokens: short chunks that the model has a numbered list of, a bit like a dictionary where every entry has a page number. The model only ever sees the page numbers.
Long numbers usually get chopped too. Many chatbots cut digits into chunks of up to three, so 500,000 might arrive as 500 · , · 000: three tokens, and nothing in them says “this 500 means five hundred thousand”. You learned place value in second grade. The model has to work it out from patterns in everything it read.
That’s one reason a chatbot can explain compound interest beautifully and still get the arithmetic wrong. Explaining is about patterns in words, which is what it’s built for. Arithmetic is about place value, which it never sees directly.

title: Lesson 1.5 (draft): How long will the money last?
text:
Open question

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text: Laura, from my drawing of Munch’s painting (1899), made to talk with Runway Act-Two. Later in the course: how.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Why are we doing this?
An AI can install software, add up numbers and write proofs faster than either of us ever will. So why learn any of it?
For the same reason people learned pure math long before anyone needed it. Almost nobody uses calculus at work. What it built was the ability to understand: to follow an argument, see why it holds, and notice when it doesn’t.
That’s the point of this course: not to get the computer to do things, but to understand what it did, and why, well enough to catch it when it’s wrong.
To check your understanding as you go, guess what each command will do before you run it. When the computer surprises you, that’s the interesting part: guess why, in your own words, check with Claude, and ask your teacher for help.






TipHow to use this page



This lesson is twelve short days, each one sitting of 15 to 30 minutes: setting up (days 1–3), Python (4–7), adding up 1 to 100 (8–10) and Lean (11–12). Do one day, stop whenever you like, and come back: the list of days at the top of the page shows where you are and takes you back there.
Each grey box has a copy button in its top right corner. Paste into the terminal with Ctrl+Shift+V and press Enter. Read the sentence above each box before you run it.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Turn on Linux (WSL)
Underneath the windows and buttons, a computer works with text. A terminal is a window where you talk to it in words. We’ll use Linux, running inside Windows (that’s WSL, Windows Subsystem for Linux).

Click Start and type PowerShell.
Right-click Windows PowerShell, choose Run as administrator, and click Yes.
Paste this and press Enter:

wsl --install
When it says so, restart the computer. A window called Ubuntu (our kind of Linux) then opens and asks you to make up a username (short, lowercase, no spaces) and a password.






WarningThe password is invisible



When you type it, nothing appears, not even dots. That’s normal. Type it anyway and press Enter.


From now on, open Terminal from the Start menu and pick Ubuntu from the ▾ menu next to the tabs.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Look around
The line ending in $ is the prompt: the computer waiting for you.
pwd
pwd prints where you are, something like /home/anna: your home folder, written as a path (folders inside folders, separated by /).
mkdir course
cd course
pwd
Before the last line, guess what pwd will print now. (mkdir makes a folder, cd goes into one, cd .. goes up a level.)

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Stop the password questions
Commands starting with sudo run as the administrator, and Linux asks for your password each time. The Windows login already protects this computer, so we tell Linux to stop asking:
echo "$USER ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/$USER
sudo chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/$USER

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Your tutor: Claude Code
Claude is an AI, a language model: it learned from a huge amount of text to predict what words come next. That turns out to be enough to explain things and write code. It also makes Claude very good at sounding right. Usually it is right. Sometimes it isn’t, and it can’t always tell. That’s why you check.
Claude Code lets you talk to Claude in the terminal. You’ll need a Claude account.
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
curl downloads the installer, and | bash runs it (the |, a pipe, sends one command’s output into the next).
Claude could do this whole lesson by itself. That’s why we tell it not to. This box writes a file called CLAUDE.md: standing instructions Claude reads every time it starts in this folder.
cat > ~/course/CLAUDE.md <<'EOF'
# Tutor mode

I'm a beginner learning to program, and above all to reason.
The point is that I work things out myself.
You're my tutor, not the one doing the work.

- Never write the code for my exercises,
  and don't run commands or edit files for me.
  If you solve it, the lesson is lost.
- If I paste an error message, explain in plain words
  what it means and where to look. One hint, not the fix.
- If I ask what a command does, explain it simply,
  then ask me to predict what will happen before I run it.
- Ask me "why?" often, and look for the hole
  in my explanations.
- If I ask how you work, or why AI gets things wrong,
  explain honestly and simply. That's part of the course.
- Allowed: if I ask for code *to referee*
  (with a hidden bug for me to find), write it.
- Keep answers short. Use everyday words.
EOF
Press Alt+Shift+D to split the window into two panes. In the right pane, start Claude:
cd ~/course
claude
The first time, it opens a browser to log in. Claude asks before it does anything on your computer: say no unless you understand what it’s asking.
Try two questions: “What did the cat > CLAUDE.md command I just ran do?” and “When are you most likely to be wrong?”
From now on: left pane, you work. Right pane, you ask.






TipAsking well



Claude only knows what you tell it. A good question says what you did, what happened, and what you think: “I ran python3 gauss.py and got this error: (paste). I think line 3 is wrong. Am I right?” Errors are normal. Read each one yourself first and guess, then paste it with your guess. Fixing it is your job.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
A friendlier shell: fish
The program that reads what you type is the shell. Ubuntu’s is bash. We’ll use fish, which helps you type less. Ask Claude what chsh does, and predict what will change, and when:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y fish
sudo chsh -s /usr/bin/fish $USER
(apt installs software.) Close the left pane (exit) and open a new one with Alt+Shift+D. Was your prediction right?
Fish suggests the rest of a command in grey from what you typed before (→ accepts it), and Tab finishes names. ↑ brings back earlier commands.
Fish doesn’t know yet where Claude was installed. Tell it once:
fish_add_path ~/.local/bin
To check your understanding (ask Claude if you’re stuck): what is a “path”, and why did bash find Claude but fish didn’t?

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
An editor: nvim
To write programs we need a text editor. nvim runs inside the terminal.
sudo apt install -y neovim
cd ~/course
nvim hello.txt
nvim has two modes, and most nvim confusion is forgetting which one you’re in:

Normal mode, where it starts: every key is a command. x deletes a letter, u undoes. Type a word here and each letter does something, usually something strange.
Insert mode: keys type letters, like any other editor. The bottom line says -- INSERT --.

i goes from normal to insert; Esc goes back. Why two modes? So every key can be a command without holding Ctrl. When in doubt, press Esc: it always lands you in normal mode, and a second press does no harm.



Press (in normal mode)
What it does




i
start typing (insert mode)


Esc
stop typing (from insert mode)


:wq Enter
save and quit


:q! Enter
quit without saving



Press i, type hello, press Esc, type :wq, press Enter. What will this print?
cat hello.txt
Everyone mistypes. In nvim, you fix things from normal mode:



Press (in normal mode)
What it does




arrow keys
move around


x
delete the letter under the cursor


u
undo (press again to undo more)


:5 Enter
jump to line 5



To add letters, move to the spot and press i; Backspace works while you’re in insert mode.
Try it: nvim hello.txt, press x. Which letter goes? Then u to bring it back. Still in normal mode, type ox. Does x delete a letter again? Decide before you read on.
o is a command too: open a new line below and switch to insert mode. So the x after it is just a letter, on a new line. Esc, then u until it’s hello again, and :wq.
Stuck in nvim? Press Esc a few times, then :q!. (More nvim: type :Tutor inside it.)

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Python
python3
The prompt changes to >>>: you’re talking to Python now. Guess each answer before pressing Enter:
2 + 2
7 / 2
7 // 2
2 ** 10
Ask Claude why 7 / 2 and 7 // 2 differ, then explain it back. Leave Python with Ctrl+D.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Boxes and questions
Start Python again and predict each line before pressing Enter:
python3
x = 5
x + 1
x
x = x + 1
x
x == 6
x == 7
x = 5 makes a box called x and puts 5 in it. x + 1 works out an answer but leaves the box alone.
In maths, x = x + 1 is nonsense. In Python, = means “work out the right side, then put it in the box on the left”.
== asks whether two things are equal, and the answer is True or False. One = stores, two == ask. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in programming.
Leave Python with Ctrl+D.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Decisions: if
cd ~/course
nvim decide.py
Type this in (i first, Esc and :wq at the end):
n = 7
if n % 2 == 0:
    print(n, "is even")
else:
    print(n, "is odd")
% is the remainder: 7 % 2 is 1. if runs the indented lines under it when its question is True, otherwise the lines under else:. What will it print? Run it:
python3 decide.py

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Typos Python can’t see
Make a typo on purpose: in decide.py, change print on line 3 to pirnt, save and run it. Will Python complain? Decide before you read on.
It doesn’t. n is 7, so line 3 never runs, and Python only notices a mistake when it gets there. Now make the same typo on line 5 and run it again: NameError: name 'pirnt' is not defined, with the line number. Fix both with the keys from Day 3: :3, :5, x and i. A program that ran once can still hide a mistake on a line it didn’t reach.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Indentation: what’s inside what
A line ending in : starts a block: the lines under it, indented 4 spaces further. The block ends at the first line that steps back out. nvim indents for you after a :, but it can’t know when a block ends. That’s you, pressing Backspace, and it’s a reasoning question: does this line belong inside?

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Copy before you change: cp
Your next program grows out of decide.py. Don’t change decide.py itself; copy it:
cp decide.py parity.py
ls
cp copies a file: first what to copy, then the new name. Now there are two, and decide.py still works whatever you do to parity.py. Every program from here on starts as a copy of the last one.
To check your understanding: what would cp parity.py decide.py do? Decide before you read on.
It would copy parity.py over decide.py. cp doesn’t ask: the old decide.py would be gone, with no undo. First name: what you have. Second name: what you’re making.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Recipes: def
nvim parity.py
Change it to this:
def parity(n):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return "even"
    else:
        return "odd"

print(7, parity(7))
print(10, parity(10))
That’s a lot of changes to a file that already exists. Six more normal-mode keys do it:



Press
What it does




dd
delete the whole line


O
open a new line above, and start typing


o
open a new line below, and start typing


>>
indent the line 4 spaces


cc
retype the whole line (its indent stays)


G
jump to the last line



Press Esc after each bit of typing:

On line 1, n = 7: dd.
O, then type def parity(n):.
Down arrow and >>, on each of the four lines under def.
On print(n, "is even"): cc, then type return "even". The same on the other print, with return "odd".
G, o, Enter for a blank line. nvim has indented the new line, guessing it is still inside the recipe. It isn’t: press Backspace once, then type the two print lines.
:wq Enter.

Gone wrong? u undoes. Or :q! and cp decide.py parity.py again: decide.py never changed, so you can always start over.
def makes a function: a recipe with a name, here parity. n is its input: a box that gets a value each time the recipe is used. return hands back the answer and ends the recipe. The recipe is the block indented under def, with the if block inside it.
Writing the recipe down doesn’t run it. parity(7) does: it puts 7 in the box n, runs the recipe and gives back what return hands it. What will the two lines say? Run it:
python3 parity.py
To check your understanding, delete the two print lines and run it again. Why does nothing appear? Decide before you read on.
The file only defines the recipe, and nothing uses it. A recipe on paper cooks nothing. Put the two lines back.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
The story
Around 1785, the story goes, a teacher told his class to add up every number from 1 to 100. A ten-year-old, Carl Friedrich Gauss, wrote the answer almost at once: 5050.
How might he have done it? Spend two minutes with a pencil before reading on.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
The slow way: a loop
A new program, so a new file (type it in yourself: typing teaches more than pasting):
cd ~/course
nvim gauss.py
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        print(k, total)
    return total

print(sum_to(100))
sum_to(n) adds up 1 to n: total starts at 0 and the loop adds each k in turn. Work out the first three lines, then run it:
python3 gauss.py
The last two lines say 100 5050, the loop’s last step, and 5050, the answer return handed back to print.
Now make an error on purpose: delete the spaces in front of total = total + k and run it. Read the error, guess what it means, then paste it to Claude with your guess.






ImportantWhy n + 1?



Change range(1, n + 1) to range(1, n). What will the last line be? Run it. An AI makes exactly this kind of mistake, and you just learned to catch it.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Gauss’s trick
Write the sum forwards and backwards:
  1 +  2 +  3 + ... +  99 + 100
100 + 99 + 98 + ... +   2 +   1
Each column adds up to 101, and there are 100 columns. Two copies of the sum make 100 × 101 = 10100, so one copy is 5050. For any \(n\):
\[1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\]
To check your understanding, explain it to Claude in your own words, without the picture, and let it look for the hole. (Does your explanation work when \(n\) is odd?)

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
A check inside the loop
assert means “this must be true here”. Try it in python3, predicting each line first:
python3
assert 4 % 2 == 0
assert 4 % 2 == 1
The first is true, so nothing happens. The second is false, and Python stops with an AssertionError. (Ctrl+D to leave.)
Now put one inside the loop, in a copy of gauss.py:
cp gauss.py invariant.py
nvim invariant.py
Replace print(k, total) with the assert (:5 Enter jumps to it, then cc):
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        assert 2 * total == k * (k + 1)
    return total

print(sum_to(100))
So this loop checks Gauss’s formula after every step. What should it print? Run it:
python3 invariant.py
It prints 5050: no step failed.
Now break the loop on purpose: change total + k to total + k + 1. At which k will the assert stop it? Then change it back.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Check lots of cases
invariant.py only checks up to 100. sum_to is a recipe, so it can run for any n. Copy invariant.py once more:
cp invariant.py check.py
nvim check.py
Replace the last line, print(sum_to(100)), with a loop over many n (G, cc; after the assert line, Backspace once, so print comes after the loop, not inside it):
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
        assert 2 * total == k * (k + 1)
    return total

for n in range(1000):
    assert 2 * sum_to(n) == n * (n + 1)
print("all 1000 agree")
The recipe is unchanged. The new loop asks, for every n from 0 to 999, whether the loop and the formula agree (twice the sum against \(n(n+1)\), so no dividing). Run it:
python3 check.py
It prints all 1000 agree. Is the formula now true for every number? Decide before you read on.
No. A thousand examples is still just examples. Mathematicians have found patterns that held for millions of cases and then broke.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Why it can never fail
A claim that stays true after every round is a loop invariant, like the assert in invariant.py. Now the big question: if the assert passed in one round, why must it pass in the next? (What does one round add to total?) Decide before you read on.
Say it passed in the round for \(k - 1\):
\[2 \cdot \text{total} = (k-1)k\]
The next round, for \(k\), adds \(k\), so \(2 \cdot \text{total}\) grows by \(2k\):
\[(k-1)k + 2k = k(k+1)\]
which is exactly what the assert checks. It passes in the first round, and each passing round makes the next one pass, so it can never fail, however far the loop runs.
That’s no longer a check. It’s a proof for every \(n\), and it’s the method from maths class: induction. The first round is the first domino, and each round knocks over the next.
Write this proof on paper, in your own words. You’ll need it on Day 12.






NoteTry it yourself




Add up the odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … and print the running total for the first 10. What pattern do you see? Why would it hold? (Try drawing it with dots.)
Ask Claude: “Write a short Python function that adds up 1 to n, with one hidden bug. Don’t tell me where.” Find the bug by reasoning first, then prove it with a check.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
section: Why AI and Lean belong together
text:
Why AI and Lean belong together
A proof that sounds right can still be wrong, and Claude is very good at sounding right. Lean doesn’t care how convincing a proof sounds: it checks every step, or it refuses. So the AI suggests, and Lean checks.
That leaves you the most important job: does the claim say what you meant? Lean checks that the proof proves the claim, not that it’s the claim you wanted.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
What Lean is
Lean is another programming language. It has boxes and loops, like Python, and it can also check proofs. Seeing the same program in a second language shows which parts are the ideas (a box, a repeat) and which are just spelling.
We’ll use Lean in the browser, with Claude beside it. Claude in Chrome is Claude in a side panel of Chrome that can read the page you’re on and type into it. Install the Claude extension from the Chrome Web Store, sign in, and pin it (the puzzle-piece icon, then the pin).
Open live.lean-lang.org, delete what’s there, and paste:
def sumLoop (n : Nat) : Nat := Id.run do
  let mut total := 0
  for k in [1:n+1] do
    total := total + k
  return total

#eval sumLoop 100
The panel on the right shows 5050. Here it is next to sum_to from gauss.py (without its print):



Python
Lean




def sum_to(n):
def sumLoop (n : Nat) : Nat :=


total = 0
let mut total := 0


for k in range(1, n + 1):
for k in [1:n+1] do


total = total + k
total := total + k


return total
return total




Nat is a natural number (0, 1, 2, …). (n : Nat) : Nat says n is one, and so is the answer.
let mut makes a box you can change (mutable).
:= puts something into a box, like Python’s =.
Id.run do says “steps, done in order”. Just copy it.
#eval runs a line and shows the answer.

To check your understanding: what does Lean make you say that Python doesn’t?

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Two programs, one answer
Gauss’s formula is a program too, a much faster one. Add it below:
def sumFormula (n : Nat) : Nat := n * (n + 1) / 2

#eval sumFormula 100
/ on natural numbers rounds down: 7 / 2 is 3. (Why doesn’t that rounding ever change the answer here?)

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
Checking isn’t proving
Do the two programs agree? Add one check, for \(n = 1000\):
#eval sumLoop 1000 == sumFormula 1000
It shows true. Now add the claim for every \(n\):
theorem agree (n : Nat) : sumLoop n = sumFormula n := by
  sorry
Read it out loud: “a claim called agree: for any natural number \(n\), the loop and the formula give the same answer. Proof: sorry.” This is check.py again, for every \(n\) instead of a thousand.
sorry means “I’ll prove this later”. Lean understands the claim but warns: declaration uses `sorry`. You still owe a proof, and checks like true don’t count. What Lean wants is an argument like your loop invariant.

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
AI translates, Lean checks
Writing Lean proofs yourself comes later in the course. Today Claude only translates your proof, and you watch what Lean says.
Open Claude in Chrome on the Lean page, type in your paper proof from Day 10, and ask:

Please prove agree in Lean by translating my proof, and see whether Lean accepts it. Don’t fix any mistakes in my proof, and don’t fix anything Lean complains about. Only translate my proof into Lean, and translate Lean’s answer back into English.

It may take a few minutes, and then Lean should accept it. Claude may add a smaller claim along the way (something like “one more round adds \(n + 1\)”). **Where is that step in your paper proof?
Next, a claim of my own. Before you send it, predict: is it true? Try \(n = 0\), 1 and 2 on paper. Then ask:

Now I want to check whether this also means that sum(n)^2 = n^3. Please convert that to Lean, have Lean check it, and translate only Lean’s answer back into English. Don’t fix the proof.

What did Lean say? And did Claude do only what you asked, or did it quietly change the claim to one that works?

title: 12 sessions: talking to the computer in words
text:
What we did today

Set up Linux with Claude as a tutor, plus fish, nvim and Python.
Added 1 to 100 with a loop and with Gauss’s trick.
Checked a thousand cases, and saw why that isn’t a proof.
Put a check inside the loop, and saw why it can never fail: induction.
Wrote the same loop in Lean, next to Gauss’s formula, and claimed the two programs always agree.
Had Claude translate your proof for Lean to check.

The computer did the adding. You did the reasoning.

title: wwhhhaattt vim 4 panel git merge???
text:
Animals on vim’s 4 panel merge screen


An early try at programming-with-cartoons, in the spirit of _why’s Poignant Guide. Current work is at home.
You don’t understand 4 panel vim merge - and git merge itself is complex - someone else’s changes, and git in a strange state. (None of which the boss is interested in.)
Luckily you can delay gratification: for example, you profit by learning basic vim editing commands, so you actually have the most powerful tool at your fingertips. Don’t take the cookie, invest about 5 more minutes - yes it looks complicated at first, but hold on, it’s actually simple and fast, and you’ll get 2 more cookies.
The bash commands you need:
git config merge.tool vimdiff git config merge.conflictstyle diff3 git config mergetool.prompt false git mergetool
You can work through this excellent example if you want to learn more details: https://www.rosipov.com/blog/use-vimdiff-as-git-mergetool/
